lines: This bridge has no steel and no nails. It's woven from grass. And every year, the villagers cut it down.
It hangs over a gorge in Peru. But grass sags within a year. So every June, four villages replace it, like they have for over five hundred years.
Step one: cord. Mountain grass called coya is hammered with stones and wet down until it's soft, then twisted by hand into thin cord.
Step two: thirty cords make one rope. Three ropes braid into one cable, as thick as a person's thigh. Then everyone hauls on it to stretch it.
Step three: the old bridge carries the new cables across. Four for the floor, two for handrails, tied to stone anchors. Then the old bridge is cut loose, and the river takes it.
Step four: two master weavers start at opposite ends, lashing handrails to floor until they meet in the middle. Then mats of branches become the deck.
Why doesn't it snap? Every cable holds ninety cords. Under your feet, three hundred sixty cords share each step, enough to carry dozens of people.
Three days later, a new bridge hangs where the old one fell. And next June, they'll cut it down and do it all again.
